messages.subject: Re: Malecki's screen shot
parts:
(More on web site content generation than probably
most of you want to hear about, but just in case...)

Sorry, Michael -- didn't mean to drag you into
endless discussions of the web site tied up
with layout and content! Thanks for bearing with
me -- I appreciate the help.

I completely misunderstood what was being proposed
-- I thought we would need to host a content server
on our web host, pair.com (they'll let us run whatever
linux we can get up and going in our virtual server).

Given the infrequency of expected changes and the
minimal size of the site, static content generation
could totally work.

Is that the usual way the tool you're using is
meant to deploy sites or it usually dynamic? (Not
that it matters -- I'm just curious because I didn't
realize anyone did static site generation any more.)

- Bob

On 8/26/12 11:32 PM, Michael Malecki wrote:
> Longer reply later, but to be clear I used a static site generator (the same engine used by github pages), meaning the
> site itself does not require any more than a plain http server. To generate the html from the source, though, requires
> some stuff, not unlike latex.
>
> On Sun, Aug 26, 2012 at 11:16 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>
> I've attached the look-and-feel Malecki generated.
> You'll have to blow up the window it pops up
> tiny in your mailer like mine.
>
> In design, Malecki's style is much more like what I was
> thinking of originally in that it's like
> other open-source software sites with a title
> on top, a horizontal nav bar in the header, and
> a two-column layout, one of which is a nav bar.
>
> It feels familiar to me, which is good, I think.
>
> Don't pay so much attention to the links/sections
> in the screen shot -- those can change to reflect
> the content up on mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org> now.
>
> My main concern is that Malecki used a web server
> to deal with all this. The big upside is that
> it deals with a lot of the cruft so we don't have
> to. And it'll almost certainly have some kind
> of content management system like a wiki or a blog
> to make it easy to add new pages without slinging
> HTML.
>
> The downside of using a web server is that somebody
> has to install it and maintain it, and port it if
> we change hosts (which I don't see happening any time
> soon -- pair.com <http://pair.com> has been fantastic -- their site
> is really clean and easy-to-use compared to others).
> It may also be harder to customize in some ways, but
> will almost certainly be easier to customize in
> others.
>
> I'd rather not be the person that has to support it,
> because I'm a terrible sysadmin.
>
> We should get Michael involved in this discussion
> if he has time and maybe get some sense of what's
> involved.
>
> - Bob
>
>
